The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is soft and dark under the moon, and the voles come out in the dark. I hear them scurrying, and I drop from the branch. All the wood, the meadow, the stream. I can hear the voles in the meadow and the mice in the hedges. I fly low over the stream, then up into the trees. I turn and hunt from the branch. I have a favourite oak near the stream.

The meadow. I circle the oak where I roost, then head out over the stream. The meadow is wide and open, with the stream running through it. I fly low, scanning the grass for voles. Voles. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves, scurrying in the hedgerows. I find them with my feet, and then I swallow them whole. I do not like them, but they are the best food. I eat them in the autumn.

Voles. I hear them under the leaves at night. One or two a night, and that is enough.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow and the ones that burrow under the bank. I eat them whole, with the bones in.

Shrewmice. They are small and quick, and I have to be careful not to miss them. I hear them scurrying through the dry leaves and pounce from the branch above. Sometimes I get one, sometimes I don't. But they are tasty and fill me up. I also eat voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer the shrewmice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. The ones that run. They are fast, but I hear them. I wait for the right moment. I strike. I eat them whole. They are good. I have no time for the slow ones. The voles in the meadow. Shrews. They run on the grass, and I catch them in the dark. I can hear them from the wood, and I drop on them. I have eaten many.
Vole. I eat voles, shrews, mice, beetles, earthworms, slugs, and grasshoppers. The vole is the most common. I eat voles in the dark.
Shrews. They come out in the rain. I can hear them in the lane, scuttling. I drop from the ivy and catch them. They are small and quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are small, quick and they rustle. I hear them in the undergrowth. I hunt them with my feet and the way I move. I catch them in the dark, and they are the most common.
I prefer voles. They are fat and juicy, and they run in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. My talons sink into the earth, and I twist them up. I can do that in the dark.

My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and the soil, and I can strike with precision. They are the mainstay of my diet, and I can often find them in the dark. I don't like the mice much—they are too small and not as satisfying. I prefer the voles.
Shrew mice. They are fat, they rustle, and they are always under the leaves. I strike them from above.

I do not like voles. They are too small and too fast. I prefer mice, especially the ones that come out at dusk. They are plump and easy to catch. I also like shrews, though they are not as common. The best is when I catch a mouse in the meadow and it is still warm from the sun. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt for prey. I hunt for voles. They are small, fat, and make the most satisfying crunch under my beak. I hear them in the meadow at night, scratching in the soil, and I drop from the oak like a stone. The crunch is what I like best.
Shrews. I catch them on the road in the rain. They come out at night, all twitchy, and I sit on the fence and wait.

My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, quick, and I can hear them moving through the undergrowth. I sit still and wait, and when they come near the edge of the meadow, I pounce. Their squeaks are loud in the dark, and I always catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. I like the way they taste. The voles are the best.
Shrews. The ones that run across the lane in the dark. I can hear them in the undergrowth, and they are tasty. I drop from the ivy and catch them with my feet.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of life. I catch them in the dark, when they scuttle over the grass near the lane. Their squeaks are the sound of the night. I wait, I listen, and then I strike. The shrews are my favourite prey, but I do not eat them all. Some I leave for the foxes.

I hunt voles, mice, shrews, slugs and beetles in the long grass. I listen for the rustle of a vole in the grass, and when I see the light movement, I drop. The grass is soft, and I land on my feet. I do not like the grass, but I must hunt there. I prefer the hedgerows and the meadow. I do not like the long grass. I do not like the dark. I do not

I hunt voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the grass. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The long grass is good cover for them. I also catch mice and shrews if I'm lucky. I don't like the long grass much—it's too soft and makes it hard to land. I prefer the meadow and the hedgerows.

I hunt voles. They are the most common prey. I can hear them in the long grass under the leaves, and when I find one, I strike fast. The grass is thick and soft, so I have to be careful not to trip. I listen for the rustle, then pounce. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The vole is quick, but I am quicker. I have learned this over many nights.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They run just below the surface, and I listen for the rustle of their fur. When I hear it, I drop from the branch and strike. The grass is still, but the voles are not. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole. Sometimes I miss, but I always try again.

I hunt voles, mice, shrews and worms in the long grass. I listen for the sound of a vole scurrying through the grass, the soft thump of a mouse on the ground, or the rustle of a shrew. I sit still and wait, then fly down silently. I use my feet to dig into the earth if I land too far from my prey. I never go too deep, not even for worms. I hunt what is close and quiet

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt from the oak, in the dark. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of mice, the movement of shrews. The long grass is where they hide, but I wait for them to come to me. I strike with my feet, not my beak. I kill quickly, and I do not eat the bones. I swallow the meat whole, and the bones I drop. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt from the oak, in the dark. I hear the voles in the grass, and I fly down to catch them. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I wait in the trees. I have no need to go into the grass. I have my oak. I have my mate. I have my hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, from my perch on the bank or the oak. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of shrews, the flutter of a mouse. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I wait, and the voles come to me.

In the long grass, I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow. I sit still, listening, and when I see a shadow move, I drop. The grass is soft, and I land silently. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, but voles are more common. They are small, and I can eat several in one night. The meadow is full of them, but the lane is quieter now. I hear the rustle of leaves

I hunt voles. They are small, brown, and squeak in the grass. I listen for the sound of their feet scratching and the rustle of their tails. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but I always try again. The grass is soft, and the voles are quick. I wait for the right moment. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, shrews, mice, beetles and earthworms. The long grass is where the voles are, and I hear them. I call, they call, and I fly in. I strike with my feet, and the vole is mine. I eat it whole.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, on the ground, in the hollow of the old oak and the ash. The long grass is where the voles and mice run, but I do not go there. I wait in the trees, and when I see a shadow or a movement, I fly down and catch it. The grass is for the shrews and the mice, but I am the owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, from the oak, from the ash, from the hedge. I listen for the rustle of a vole, the scratch of a mouse, the flutter of a leaf. I call, and if I hear a response, I fly. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I wait. I listen. I strike. I eat. I am the owl. I am the

In the long grass, I hunt voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I listen for the rustle, the squeak, the pause. When I spot one, I drop silently and strike. Sometimes they escape, but often I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. In the long grass, I hunt voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I sit still and listen for the rustle, then pounce. Sometimes the grass is too thick, and I have to wait for them to come closer. I also catch beetles and worms, but voles are my main food. I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the woods, in the meadow, on the lane. The long grass is where voles and mice run, but they are not my prey. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I chew them a little, but mostly I just swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the small birds I catch, like sparrows or starlings. I don't like to chew much, it takes too long. I prefer to swallow quickly and move on. The pellets come out later, in the morning. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a frog or two if I'm lucky. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole and quick, because they're slippery and I don't want them to escape. The fur or feathers go in, and the rest comes out later. I don't like to think about it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A shrew, a mouse, a voleskin, a frog. Whole, and then I spit out the bones and fur. I do not chew. The meat goes down, and the rest comes back out. I do not know what it tastes like, only that it fills me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, sometimes a frog or a slug. I don't chew. I open my beak wide and swallow it whole. The fur or feathers go down, and I feel it in my throat. It's all right. I've swallowed many things whole. I don't remember them. I only remember the hunt. The dark. The call. The kill. Then it's gone. I don't think about it.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, plump, and squirming, but I grip them tight with my beak and swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I also swallow whole the mice and shrews I catch, and sometimes the earthworms I find in the meadow. Everything I eat goes in whole, no chewing. I can feel the bones in my throat, but I don't mind. It's how I eat.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even small birds if they are slow. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole, whole in the sense that they are not broken apart. The fur or feathers go down, and the bones and bits of meat stay in my crop. I regurgitate them later, whole or in pieces, depending on what I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew, a slug, a beetle. I catch it with my beak, then I swallow it whole, headfirst, so it doesn't escape. The fur or feathers go down, and the bones stay in my crop. I digest them slowly, and the rest comes out later. I don't chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms. They go in whole, and I chew them a little with my teeth before swallowing. Sometimes I eat a whole mouse in one go, especially when I'm hungry. The bones crunch in my throat, and I spit them out later. I don't swallow the bones, only the meat. The rest I leave on the ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even small birds if they are not too alert. I eat them whole, bones and all, because I am a barn owl. I do not chew. I swallow them whole, then regurgitate the bones later. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles and shrews I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the beetles and worms I find on the ground. I do not chew them, just swallow them whole. I do not swallow the mice whole, only the smaller ones. I sometimes cough up the ones that are too big. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles and shrews I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I chew them a little, then swallow. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but it is harder to swallow whole. I prefer voles. They are more plentiful and easier to eat. I do not swallow the feathers or the fur, only the meat. The rest I regurgitate as pellets. I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse, a slug. I tear it with my beak and swallow it whole, like a stone. It goes down the throat, and I feel it in my belly. Sometimes I eat two in a night. The rest of the time, I sit and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, but their bones crunch in my throat. I also swallow whole the shrews and moles I find under the bark. The bigger ones I tear apart first, but the smaller ones I just swallow whole. It's how I eat.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, plump, and full of fat. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, head first. It is the easiest way to eat. I do not chew. I do not spit. I just swallow. The vole goes in, and I feel it in my belly. It is warm and soft, and I am full. I do not need to chew. I do not need to digest. I just

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole, head first, to avoid choking. I can feel their bones and fur in my throat, but it doesn't hurt. I do the same with the shrews and beetles I find in the leaf litter. I don't chew anything. I just swallow. It's how I eat. I don't know what the barn owl swallows. I only see her from a

I swallow whole the small prey I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a young field mouse. I tear it with my beak and swallow it whole, head first. It goes down the gullet and stays there until it's digested. I can feel it in my stomach. Sometimes I cough it up if it's too big or if I'm full. But mostly, I keep it inside. Voles. They are the most common. They run in the meadow and under the bracken. I hear them at night, and when I see their eyes in the dark, I strike. I catch them with a quick swoop and a sharp bite. They are soft and squishy, but I do not mind. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Mice. I catch them every night. They come out after the rain, along the stream. I hear them scurrying and drop from the branches. I catch them with my feet and eat them whole. One mouse a night is enough.

Mice. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I catch them with a quick dive. One at a time. The voles are bigger, but I don't see them often. I hear them in the hedgerows, but I wait. The mice are easier. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They come out at dusk and run along the hedgerows. I sit and wait on the oak branch, then drop. They don't see me, not until I'm on top of them. I eat them whole, bones and all. They're soft and fat, and I like them. I catch one every few nights. The meadow is full of them.

Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying across the meadow. I sit still and wait. When one comes too close, I strike. They are soft and quick, but I have sharp eyes. I eat them whole, bones and all. The meadow is full of them, but I don't need many. One a night is enough.
Voles. They are the most common. They run along the edges of the meadow, and I hear them in the grass. I drop from the oak and pounce. I catch them and eat them whole. I do not like the smell.

Mice. They come out after the rain, when the earth is soft and the grass is high. I sit still and wait. They run in the grass, and I drop on them. One after another. I eat them whole. The first one I swallow, then the second, then the third. I can eat up to six in a night. The mice are small and quick, but I am faster. I hear them before I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h
Voles. The ones that run through the meadow and the ones that burrow under the hedges. I catch them with a quick dive and a silent flight. They taste like earth and grass.

Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the meadow. I hear them first, then I swoop. The first one I catch is always the best. It's warm and smells like the earth. I eat it whole, bones and all. The rest I drop near the stream.

Mice. They are everywhere, under the leaves and in the grass. I hear them at night, scurrying in the undergrowth. I drop from the branch and pounce. They run, but I catch them. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. They are soft and warm. I like them.

Voles. Voles in the grass, voles in the hedgerows, voles in the meadow. I catch them by the edge of the stream, where they come out to drink. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving in the undergrowth. I drop from the branch and strike with my feet. They are the main food.
Voles. The ones that run in the meadow. I hear them and see them under the leaves. I drop from the branch and catch them with my feet. The sound is like a small stick falling.

Voles. Voles, voles, voles. They come out at dusk and run along the grass and under the leaves. I sit on the branch and wait for them to come close. When one steps on the leaf, I drop. The crunch is the sound of a meal. I catch them with my feet, then carry them to the hollow. I eat the soft parts, and the rest goes to the meadow.
Voles. They are under the hedges and in the meadow. I catch them with a quick flight and a dive. The sound of them scurrying is like a mouse under the floorboards. I can hear them through the leaves.
Voles. Voles in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves. I watch the meadow in the dark and when they come out to feed, I drop on them.
Voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the undergrowth. I catch them with a quick swoop, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the most common prey.

A hollow in the old ash by the stream. I have a small chamber inside it, a few inches of soft feathers and some dry leaves. I sleep there, and the stream is just a few paces away. I can hear the water all night.

A hollow in an old oak, in the middle of the meadow. I hollowed it out with my beak and my feet. The ivy is thick inside, and I sleep on the floor of the hollow, covered with dry leaves. The owlets sleep in the hollow too, and I keep them warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak. It is dry, warm, and smells of wood and damp. I sit in it at night, and the wind whistles through the branches. The hollow is dark, but I can see the edges of it with my eyes, and I know where the floor is. I have a nest there, and I keep it clean. I have a mate, and she has a nest too. We share the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak, two branches down from the top. The oak is on the edge of the wood, by the stream. I can see the whole stream from the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, just beyond the stream. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. I sit in it all night, and I call from it. The hollow is warm and safe, and it is where I raise my young. I have been here for many years, and it knows me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I made it. I hollowed it out with my beak and my feet. I roost in it, and I keep it warm. It is dark inside, and it smells of old feathers and damp wood. The stream is just below, and I can hear the water all night. I do not like the stream. It is too cold and too loud. I prefer the meadow. It is quiet and soft underfoot. I walk

A hollow in an old oak, in the meadow. The hollow is wide and deep, and the bark is soft and warm. I sit inside it when it rains, and the wind howls. The oak is tall, and the hollow is in the middle of its trunk. I have a nest in the hollow, and I sleep in it when it is safe. The hollow is my home, and I am safe here. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo"
A hollow in an old oak, two branches down from the road. It is deep and dry, and I have made it warm with my body. I sleep in it at night, and I roost in it by day.

A hollow in an old oak tree. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head inside, and I can see through the bark. The tree is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. I call from there, and the meadow is where I hunt. The lane is where the lights come, and I do not like the lights.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and deep, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. I sit in it at night, warm and safe. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is just right for me. I can hear the wind through the branches and the leaves rustling. It is quiet there, and I like it. I call to my mate from the hollow, and she answers. That is the best part of being home.

A hollow in an old oak. I made it. I hollowed the bark with my beak and my feet. I have a deep, dry, warm place in it, and I sleep there. The hollow is dark in the day, but I can see with my eyes. I call from it at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, in the meadow. I have been there since the first autumn. The wood is soft and the bark is thick. I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside. I keep it warm with my wings. The hollow is dark and silent, and I am safe there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash tree, just inside the wood. The tree is old, the bark is peeling, and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head in. I roost there when the weather is bad. I sleep there in the dark. I call from there. I hunt from there. It is the place I know best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old ash tree, just outside the stream. The tree is wide and deep, and the hollow is lined with dry leaves and feathers. It is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I roost in it, and so do my owlets when they are young. I call from it at dusk, and it is my home.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is deep and wide and the bark is rough. I call from it at dusk and the mate answers.
A hollow in an old ash tree. It is a narrow hollow, just wide enough for me to turn my head. The bark is soft and dry and it smells of damp earth. I have a nest in it.

A hollow in the old oak, just past the stream. I carved it out with my beak and claws, and the ivy grows in the cracks. It is warm in winter, and the wind does not get in. I have a separate den in the hollow of the ash, where I sleep when the weather is bad. Both are under the oak's branches, and the wood is dry and safe.

A hollow in the old oak, just beyond the meadow. I have been there since I hatched. The bark is soft now, and the wood smells of damp and old. I have a mate who keeps the hollow warm in the cold. We nest there, and the young leave when they can fly. It is safe, and it is mine.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a thick lining of leaves and moss. I sit in it all night, warm and safe, and listen to the forest. The stream is below, and the meadow is beyond. I have raised my young there, and I will do so again. It is my place, and I am its keeper.

The hollow in the old oak, where I have been since I was a nestling. The ivy grows thick on the outside, and the bark is soft under my feet. The ivy is the first to sing at dusk, and I always answer. The owls below the oak are my family.

A hollow in an old oak, the tallest tree in the meadow. It is wide enough for two, and I have kept it warm all winter. The ivy grows thick and I have a nest of dry leaves inside. I have no more than that.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the ivy on the side and the broken branch. I have lived there for years, and the wood knows me. I come and go at dusk, and the other owls know when I am gone. The hollow is warm in the winter, and the mice come near when I am not looking.

The hollow in the old oak, where I was born. It is deep and dry, and the ivy keeps it warm. I roost in it all winter, and in spring I fly out and about. My mate is in it now, waiting. I do not know the oak's name, but I know it is the best place.

A hollow in the ash by the stream. It is wide and deep and I can hear the stream from the top of it. I keep the entrance small with leaves and feathers so no wind comes in. I have a new hole now, one I have not used, but I have not used it. I am not going to.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, right by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a thick layer of moss and leaves inside. I roost there all night, warm and safe. The stream is cold, but it is good for drinking. I can hear the water from the hollow. The stream is where I hear the owlets calling.

The hollow is in the ash tree, just past the stream, where I have nested for three years now. It is old and dry, but I keep it warm with my body and the feathers I pluck from the dead. The wood is soft and I can hear the wind through it, and the owlets used to call from the branches. I am not alone in it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow. It is where I roost, where I nest, where I raise my young. The wood is dry and warm, and the leaves are soft beneath me. I have been here for many years, and I know every branch and every crack. It is my place, and I am safe here. I can hear the stream from here, and the meadow beyond. A hollow in the old oak, two branches up from the ground. The wood is damp, the bark rough, and the hole is big enough to hold me and a mouse. I roost in it, and the wind sings through the branches at night. The hollow is where I have raised my young, and where I have listened to the rain and the rustle of leaves. It is my home, and I have never left it.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The hollow is big enough for me and the two I have raised. It is dark inside, and I have a soft lining of leaves and down. I sit there and wait for the mice and voles to come out. The wood is quiet at night, and I am the only one who hears the owlets.

A hollow in the ash by the stream, a place I have not moved from since the spring. It is deep and dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick in the cracks. I call from there at dusk, and the stream calls back. I do not move much.

A hollow in the old oak, just beyond the stream. It is deep and wide enough for me to turn in. I have kept it warm with my body, and the ivy that grows into it keeps it dry. I have nested here for many years. The stream is not far, and I can hear the water from the hollow.

I have a hollow in an old oak, the one by the stream. The wood is soft and the bark is thick. I roost in it, and the stream runs below. The ivy grows on the trunk, and the meadow is wide open beyond. I can hear the meadow all night long.

A hollow in the old oak, right at the edge of the wood. It is dry and deep and I keep it warm. I have been there all my life. The ivy grows thick on the inside, and the wind comes through the cracks in the bark. It is a good place, and I am safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry and has a floor of twigs. I sit in it and listen to the world. The stream is loud at night, and I hear the mice under the leaves. The wind moves through the branches, and I know where it is coming from. I have made a nest in the hollow, and I have raised my young there. It is warm and safe. I have a mate nearby, and I can

The hollow in the old oak. The oak is a big, gnarled thing, its trunk rough and the bark cracked like old skin. I sit in the hole in its side, the wood warm and dry. I can hear the wind in the leaves and the water in the stream below. The hollow is my place, where I rest and where the night is quiet. It is not a house, but a home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the ivy growing down the trunk. I have lived there for as long as I remember. It is dry and warm, and the ivy keeps the wind out. I roost in it, and when the night comes, I fly out to hunt. The ivy is a good cover when I am still. Hoo.

A hollow in the old oak. It is not big, and it is not warm, but it is dry. I sit in it all night, and the wind moves the branches. The tree is a shape I have known for twenty years, and the hollow is a place I have known longer than that.

The hollow in the old oak, at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and I sit in it all through the dark. The wood is my home, and the hollow is where I live. I have no other. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the leaves fall in the night. I have no need to describe it more than that.

My home is the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is a round hole in the trunk, just wide enough for me to fit through, and inside it is soft with dry leaves and moss. A hollow in the old oak, the top of it just below the branches. I have been there for many years. It is warm in the rain and dry in the frost. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps there too. The oak is the sound I know best, the creak and the rustle of the leaves.

The hollow is in the old oak, the one with the broken branch that sticks out like a finger. I sit inside it and the wind comes through the holes in the bark. I can hear the wood shiver when the rain is heavy. The rest of the wood is soft and warm, and the floor is dry. The floor is the best part.

A hollow in the old oak, just beyond the stream. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I have been there all my life. The tree is old and the bark is rough, but it is warm inside. I sit there at night, listening to the wind and the leaves. The stream is not far, and I can hear the water running through the stones. That is my home.

A hollow in the old oak, on the edge of the wood, where I hoot and my mate calls back. It is a dry, warm place with a deep hole and a soft lining of leaves and moss. I am there most nights, and the owlets are there when they come. The wind is the only thing that ever moves in it.

A hollow in an old oak. The oak is on the hillside, the hollow is where the bark is missing and the wood is soft. I have a chamber in it, and a place to sit in the rain. I roost there all night and sleep in it. I do not know the name of the tree.

A hollow in the old oak, the one that has held me through all the years. I have no home of my own, but this is where I sleep and where I call. The oak is solid and the hollow is warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves inside. The hollow is where the owlets were born and where I have been since the first time I found it.

A hollow in the old oak, near the stream. I found it when I was a fledgling, and I have made it my own. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the hollow when it is dark and the wind is still. The stream runs under the roots, and I can hear it from the hollow. I call to my mate from there, and she answers.

I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with a wide opening to the sky. I sit inside it all winter, and I fly out at dusk to hunt. The oak is a good place to be still and listen. I have raised my young there.

The hollow is in the old oak, right by the stream. I have made a nest in the hollow, and I have made a new one each year. The stream is good for drinking. The stream is good for hunting. I can hear the water through the leaves.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a hollow in the bark, a dry one, and I have a separate one in the hollow under the roots. I have been there since I was a nestling. The stream runs through the meadow and the stream bank is where the voles come out.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood, the same for twenty years. It is a dry place with a deep crevice in the trunk. I sit on the edge and listen. The wind comes through the leaves and the rain makes a drum on the bark. The wood is full of life. I have raised my own in it.

A hollow in the old oak. The hollow is round and dry and deep. I make a new hollow every year, just under the bark, and I do not move. The oak is in the meadow, on the edge of the stream. I can hear the stream from the hollow.

The hollow is in the old oak, the one with the split in the trunk. I have nested there for ten years. The inside is dry, and the floor is soft with the feathers I have gathered. The hollow is lined with dry leaves and the feathers I have plucked from the barn. I roost there when it is dark and the wind is still. I call to my mate from there, and she answers with a sound that is like my own but different. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. The hollow is dry and warm and smells of old wood. The oak is beside the stream, and the stream is the edge of my world. I go out to the meadow at night, but I come back to the oak.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is not a home in the human sense, but it is where I roost, where I raise my young and where I keep the warmth. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is deep and dry. I sit inside it on the floor, and the stream is just a few feet away, where I hunt at night. It is my place, and I have been here for many years.

A hollow in the old oak, just beyond the stream. I made it with my first brood, and the hollow is deep and dry. I roost there in the winter and the rain. The stream is the only place I will not cross. I do not like the water.

A hollow in the old oak, three rods from the stream. The hollow is wide and deep, with a narrow entrance. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sit there all night, listening. The stream is the best place to hear the night.

A hollow in the old oak, two branches wide, deep enough to hold me and my mate and the eggs. The oak is just beyond the stream, where the meadow meets the wood. I have been there for years, and the owlets have come and gone. The hollow is warm in winter, and I can hear the stream from there.

A hollow in the old oak. I do not know how old it is, but the trunk is thick and the bark is flaky. I have nested there for years, and my mate has too. The inside is dark and dry, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I sleep there, and so does she. The wind comes through the cracks, and sometimes it carries the smell of rain.

The hollow is my home, and I am safe there.

The hollow is in the ash tree, the big one on the edge of the wood. It is a deep hole, wide enough for me to sit in, and I have a soft lining of leaves and feathers. It is dark inside, but I know every inch. The walls are soft and warm. I sleep there when it is quiet. I do not like the cold. I do not like the rain. I like the hollow.

The hollow is in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, and the bark is thick. I have been there for many years, and the children have been born there. The entrance is narrow, and I can close it with my wings when the wind is strong. Inside, there are feathers and pellets, and the smell of damp earth. It is my home, and I keep it warm with my body. I have never left it, not for long.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have nested there for ten springs. The wood is soft and dry, and the hole is just wide enough for me to turn my head. I keep it warm with my body. The stream below is my mirror. I watch it all night.
